title: E2: 2-bromopropane and ethoxide
subtitle: A strong base removes HBr in one step

reactants.caption: sodium ethoxide + 2-bromopropane
reactants.learnerPrompt: Ethoxide is a strong base. Draw the E2 elimination in one step.
hintTiers: Which hydrogens can a base remove so that a C=C bond forms where the C–Br bond was? They sit on a carbon next to the one carrying bromine.
Three arrows at once: the oxygen takes the drawn hydrogen, that C–H bond becomes the new π bond, and the C–Br bond breaks onto bromine.
Oxygen lone pair → the drawn hydrogen; the C–H bond → a π bond between the two carbons; the C–Br bond → a lone pair on bromine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That is SN2 substitution, and it does happen here (about 20%). But on a secondary carbon a strong base like ethoxide mostly removes a proton: draw the elimination.
Ethoxide and bromine are both electron-rich. The base attacks a hydrogen, not the bromine.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right start: the base takes the proton. Now the C–H electrons need somewhere to go: into a new C=C π bond, which pushes bromide out.
Bromide does leave, but not on its own here: with a strong base everything happens in one step. Add the base taking the proton and the C–H electrons forming the π bond.

steps.explanationAfterStep: One concerted step. The C–H and C–Br bonds that break are anti-periplanar, so the C–H orbital lines up with the back of the C–Br bond and the π bond forms smoothly.

mechanismSummary: Ethoxide takes a hydrogen from a carbon next to the C–Br carbon (a β-hydrogen). In the same step the C–H electrons form the C=C π bond and bromide leaves. The H and Br that leave are anti-periplanar: on opposite sides of the C–C bond, in one plane. Propene is about 80% of the product; the rest is the SN2 ether, ethyl isopropyl ether.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 17
